Big Data Processing Frameworks
● Big data processing frameworks are software tools that are specifically 
designed to handle the processing and analysis of large and complex data 
sets. 
● These frameworks are built to scale horizontally, meaning they can easily 
handle massive amounts of data by distributing the workload across 
multiple nodes or servers. 
● This allows companies to process and analyze data in real-time, enabling 
them to make faster and more accurate decisions.
● Big data processing frameworks are essential tools for businesses looking 
to harness the power of their data.

Big Data Processing Frameworks
● There are several popular big data processing frameworks available in the 
market today.
● Each has its own unique features and capabilities. 
● Some of the most commonly used frameworks include Apache Hadoop, 
Apache Spark, and Apache Flink. 
● These frameworks are open-source and offer a wide range of tools and 
libraries to help companies process and analyze their data effectively.
● Modern big data processing often occurs in cloud environments due to 
scalability and cost-efficiency.

Apache Spark
● Apache Spark is an open source distributed data processing engine that 
enables users to perform complex data analysis across large datasets. 
● It is a multi-language engine for executing data engineering, data science, 
and machine learning on single-node machines or clusters.
● It is designed to be fast, flexible and easy to use, making it suitable for 
various applications in data science and analytics.
● It utilizes in-memory caching, and optimized query execution for fast 
analytic queries against data of any size.
● It provides development APIs in Java, Scala, Python and R, and supports 
code reuse across multiple workloads—batch processing, interactive 
queries, real-time analytics, machine learning, and graph processing.

Apache Spark
Features of Apache Spark
1. In-memory computing
2. Unified analytics
3. Support for multiple languages (Polyglot programming)
4. Built-in libraries
5. Fault tolerance- through Resilient Distributed Datasets (RDDs)
6. Lazy evaluation
7. Advanced DAG execution engine

Apache Spark
Benefits of Apache Spark
● Fast- Through in-memory caching, and optimized query execution
● Developer friendly- a variety of languages for building your applications. 
These APIs make it easy for the developers
● Multiple workloads- the ability to run multiple workloads, including 
interactive queries, real-time analytics, machine learning, and graph 
processing.
● Real-time processing- with Structured Streaming and the legacy Spark 
Streaming.
● Scalability and fault tolerance
● Extensive library support

Apache Spark
Apache Spark Workloads
The Spark framework includes:
● Spark Core as the foundation for the platform
● Spark SQL for interactive queries
● Spark Streaming for real-time analytics
● Spark MLlib for machine learning
● Spark GraphX for graph processing

Apache Spark
Apache Spark Workloads

Apache Spark
Apache Spark Workloads
Spark Core
● Spark Core is the foundation of the platform. 
● It is responsible for memory management, fault recovery, scheduling, 
distributing & monitoring jobs, and interacting with storage systems. 
● Spark Core is exposed through an application programming interface 
(APIs) built for Java, Scala, Python and R. 
● These APIs hide the complexity of distributed processing behind simple, 
high-level operators.

Apache Spark
Apache Spark Workloads
MLlib- Machine Learning
● Spark includes MLlib, a library of algorithms to do machine learning on 
data at scale. Machine Learning models can be trained by data scientists 
with R or Python on any Hadoop data source, saved using MLlib, and 
imported into a Java or Scala-based pipeline. Spark was designed for fast, 
interactive computation that runs in memory, enabling machine learning 
to run quickly. The algorithms include the ability to do classification, 
regression, clustering, collaborative filtering, and pattern mining.

Apache Spark
Apache Spark Workloads
Spark Streaming- Real-time
● Spark Streaming is a real-time solution that leverages Spark Core’s fast 
scheduling capability to do streaming analytics. It ingests data in 
mini-batches, and enables analytics on that data with the same 
application code written for batch analytics. This improves developer 
productivity, because they can use the same code for batch processing, 
and for real-time streaming applications. Spark Streaming supports data 
from Twitter, Kafka, Flume, HDFS, and ZeroMQ, and many others found 
from the Spark Packages ecosystem.

Apache Spark
Apache Spark Workloads
Spark SQL- Interactive Queries
● Spark SQL is a distributed query engine that provides low-latency, 
interactive queries up to 100x faster than MapReduce. It includes a 
cost-based optimizer, columnar storage, and code generation for fast 
queries, while scaling to thousands of nodes. Business analysts can use 
standard SQL or the Hive Query Language for querying data. Developers 
can use APIs, available in Scala, Java, Python, and R. It supports various 
data sources out-of-the-box including JDBC, ODBC, JSON, HDFS, Hive, 
ORC, and Parquet. Other popular stores—Amazon Redshift, Amazon S3, 
Couchbase, Cassandra, MongoDB, Salesforce.com, Elasticsearch, and 
many others can be found from the Spark Packages ecosystem.

Apache Spark
Apache Spark Workloads
GraphX- Graph Processing
● Spark GraphX is a distributed graph processing framework built on top of 
Spark. GraphX provides ETL, exploratory analysis, and iterative graph 
computation to enable users to interactively build, and transform a graph 
data structure at scale. It comes with a highly flexible API, and a selection 
of distributed Graph algorithms.

Apache Spark
Applications of Apache Spark
● Financial Services
Spark is used in banking to predict customer churn, and recommend new financial 
products. 
In investment banking, Spark is used to analyze stock prices to predict future trends.
● Healthcare
Spark is used to build comprehensive patient care, by making data available to 
front-line health workers for every patient interaction. Spark can also be used to 
predict/recommend patient treatment.
● Manufacturing
Spark is used to eliminate downtime of internet-connected equipment, by 
recommending when to do preventive maintenance.
● Retail
Spark is used to attract, and keep customers through personalized services and offers.

NoSQL Databases
● A NoSQL (non-relational) database stores and manages large volume of 
data in flexible, non-tabular formats.
● Also known as purpose-built databases.
● They don’t rely on predefined schemas, allowing for greater adaptability 
as data evolves.
● Apart from structured data, they can also handle semi-structured and 
unstructured data.

NoSQL Databases
Features of NoSQL databases
● Schema-free design: No fixed structure, allowing flexible and dynamic 
data models. 
● Horizontal scalability: Easily distributes data across multiple servers for 
growth. 
● Optimized performance: Excellent for fast read/write operations. 
● Handles unstructured data: Works efficiently with text, images, videos, 
and logs.
NoSQL Databases

NoSQL Databases
Types of NoSQL databases
● Document databases: Store data in JSON or BSON-like documents with 
flexible fields. Examples include MongoDB and Couchbase.
● Key-value stores: Store data as unique keys paired with values, ideal for 
caching and sessions. Examples include Redis and Amazon DynamoDB.
● Wide-column stores: Store data in flexible rows and dynamic columns for 
large distributed workloads. One example is Apache Cassandra.
● Graph databases: Store data as nodes and edges to map highly connected 
relationships. One example is Neo4j.

NoSQL Databases
Types of NoSQL databases

NoSQL Databases
Advantages of NoSQL databases
● High flexibility
● High scalability
● High performance
● High availability
● Supports diverse data types

NoSQL Databases
Trade-offs
● Less structure: Querying complex data can be more challenging. 
● Limited ACID compliance: Some NoSQL systems prioritize speed over 
strict consistency. 
● Younger ecosystem: SQL databases offer more mature tools and 
documentation. 
● Higher management needs: Indexing and optimization often require 
manual tuning.

NoSQL Databases: Key-Value Stores
● Key-value databases store data as pairs of keys and values. 
● Each key is a unique identifier (like a name, ID, or reference number) 
● and is associated with a value, which can be anything from a simple string 
to a more complex data structure, such as an object or a list.

NoSQL Databases: Key-Value Stores
● To retrieve data, the database management system looks up the value 
using the associated key. 
● For example, you request the value for "K2." The database applies a hash 
function to that key, retrieves the value from the computed location, and 
returns the value "AAA, BBB."
● Key-value databases are optimized for fast, efficient, and simple lookups
by key, but they are limited when it comes to complex query operations. 
● For example, you can’t filter the values based on attributes like “find all 
users with ages greater than 30” because the system only stores and 
retrieves data based on the unique key.

NoSQL Databases: Key-Value Stores
Key-value database use cases
Key-value databases excel due to their flexibility and speed in various scenarios.
Popular Key-value databases: Redis, Memcached, RocksDB, Hazelcast, Valkey

NoSQL Databases: Column-Oriented Databases
● Сolumn-oriented (or wide-column) databases store data column by 
column rather than rows, organizing related information in column 
families. 
● Unlike SQL databases, the structure of these columns doesn’t have to be 
consistent across rows. 
● Each row within a family can have a completely different number of 
columns. 
● This flexibility allows column-oriented databases to handle large amounts 
of data with varying schemas.
NoSQL Databases: Column-Oriented Databases

NoSQL Databases: Column-Oriented Databases
From the image above, the data is organized as follows.
"1" is the partition key, which uniquely identifies the row.
"Book ID" is the sort key, which organizes data within a partition.
"1984," “George Orwell,” and “1949” are attributes that store additional data associated 
with the row. A new attribute or column can be added to a row without requiring all 
rows to include it.
Wide-column databases support complex queries like filtering, grouping, and 
aggregating over massive datasets with millions or billions of rows.

NoSQL Databases: Column-Oriented Databases
Column-Oriented database use cases
Column-oriented databases are particularly useful in analytical and large-scale applications.
Popular Column-Oriented databases: Apache Cassandra, Apache HBase,
Apache Druid, ScyllaDB

NoSQL Databases: Document Databases
● Document databases store, manage, and retrieve data in the form of 
documents (in JSON, BSON, or XML formats). 
● Each document is identified by a unique key (similar to the key in a 
key-value store) and contains relevant information about a particular 
entity (for example, product order). 
● Data within each document can be organized in nested fields, arrays, and 
other structures.
NoSQL Databases: Document Databases

NoSQL Databases: Document Databases
● Documents have no predefined schema, allowing for flexibility in how 
data is represented.
● For example, in an SQL database, a "patients" table would require all 
records to have the same columns, such as "name," "age," and "address." 
● In a document, each patient's record can be customized—some may 
include additional fields like "allergies" or "ongoing treatments."

NoSQL Databases: Document Databases
● Document databases allow you to query information not just by the 
unique identifier (like the key in key-value databases) but also by the 
internal content. 
● You can apply conditions or filters to your queries. 
● For example, you can find all users within a certain age group or of a 
certain status.
● Document databases also support aggregation operations (calculating, 
grouping, and summarizing data) and indexing (locating and retrieving 
documents based on the indexed fields).

NoSQL Databases: Document Databases
Document database use cases
Popular Document databases: MongoDB, Apache CouchDB, Firebase
Firestore, Amazon DocumentDB

NoSQL Databases: Graph Databases
● Graph databases are designed to store, manage, and query data in the 
form of graphs that consist of nodes and edges

NoSQL Databases: Graph Databases
Graph components:
● Nodes (or vertices) represent entities (e.g., people, products, locations).
● Edges are the relationships between nodes (e.g., "friend with," "purchased 
from," "located at").
● Properties store additional information (e.g., a "friend with" relationship 
could have a "since" property to indicate when the relationship was 
established).
An edge always has a start node, end node, type, and direction. It can describe 
parent-child relationships, actions, ownership, and the like. There is no limit to 
the number and kind of relationships a node can have.

NoSQL Databases: Graph Databases
● One of the key features of graph databases is their ability to efficiently 
traverse relationships between nodes. 
● For example, if you want to find all users who are friends of friends of a 
particular user, a graph database will allow you to follow the "friendship" 
edges. 
● A query will start at one node and follow a chain of relationships to reach 
other connected nodes.

NoSQL Databases: Graph Databases
● Graph databases excel at managing highly interconnected data and 
● allow for intuitive, flexible queries, making them powerful for modern 
applications involving complex relationships.

NoSQL Databases: Graph Databases
Graph database use cases
Popular Graph databases: Neo4j, Amazon Neptune, JanusGraph

NoSQL Databases: Multi-model Databases
● Multi-model databases: Integrate multiple NoSQL database types into a 
single system to handle diverse data models and queries.
● Multi-model databases support different ways of storing data (document, 
key-value, graph, and wide-column) within the same system. 
● They allow applications to store data in the most convenient form, 
handling only one repository. 
● For example, user data can be kept as documents and relations as 
graphs.

NoSQL Databases: Multi-model Databases
Popular Multi-model databases: Amazon DynamoDB, Couchbase, Azure
Cosmos DB, ArangoDB
● Amazon DynamoDB supports document and key-value models.
● Couchbase combines the functionality of a document and key-value store
with built-in operational and analytical capabilities.
● ArangoDB embraces graph, document, and key-value data models.
● Azure Cosmos DB supports storing data in documents, key-value pairs,
wide columns, and graphs.

BDA in Business Intelligence and Decision Support Systems
● Big Data Analytics is not just about handling large datasets—it’s about 
turning raw data into strategic intelligence. 
● When integrated with BI and DSS, it empowers organizations to predict, 
personalize, optimize, and innovate. 
● For businesses, adopting BDA-driven BI can enhance competitiveness in 
retail, finance, and healthcare sectors, where data-driven decisions are 
increasingly critical.

BDA in Business Intelligence and Decision Support Systems
● Big Data Analytics (BDA) is transforming Business Intelligence (BI) and 
Decision Support Systems (DSS) by 
○ enabling organizations to uncover hidden insights, improve decision accuracy, 
reduce costs, and gain competitive advantage. 
● Its applications span finance, healthcare, manufacturing, retail, and 
beyond, with AI-driven tools amplifying the impact.

BDA in Business Intelligence and Decision Support Systems
● Big Data Analytics (BDA) is transforming Business Intelligence (BI) and 
Decision Support Systems (DSS) by 
○ enabling organizations to uncover hidden insights, improve decision accuracy, 
reduce costs, and gain competitive advantage. 
● Its applications span finance, healthcare, manufacturing, retail, and 
beyond, with AI-driven tools amplifying the impact.

Applications of Big Data Analytics in BI & DSS
● BI → Focuses on reporting, visualization, and insights for operational and 
tactical decisions.
● DSS → Focuses on structured decision-making support with simulations, 
optimization, and predictive modeling for strategic choices.

Applications of Big Data Analytics in BI
● Real-Time Dashboards: Continuous monitoring of KPIs (sales, customer 
engagement, supply chain metrics).
● Predictive Analytics for Market Trends: Anticipating demand, seasonal 
fluctuations, and consumer behavior.
● Customer Segmentation & Personalization: Using purchase history, 
browsing data, and social media to tailor offers.
● Fraud Detection & Risk Monitoring: Identifying anomalies in transactions 
and user behavior.
● Performance Benchmarking: Comparing business units, products, or 
regions using large-scale data.
● Marketing Optimization: Tracking campaign effectiveness and adjusting 
strategies dynamically.

Applications of Big Data Analytics in DSS
● Scenario Modeling & Simulation: Testing “what-if” conditions (e.g., policy 
changes, pricing strategies).
● Resource Allocation Optimization: Deciding how to distribute staff, funds, 
or inventory efficiently.
● Healthcare Decision Support: Predicting patient outcomes, supporting 
diagnosis, and treatment planning.
● Financial Portfolio Management: Integrating structured (stock prices) and 
unstructured (news sentiment) data.
● Policy & Strategic Planning: Governments and enterprises simulate 
long-term outcomes for urban planning, energy use, or climate strategies.
● Crisis Management: Real-time DSS for disaster response, epidemic 
tracking, or supply chain disruptions.
